summary:
Haryāna stands under the national framework of India. No Haryāna-specific transgender statute, enforcement series or incident pattern with a source was identified, so a visitor's expectations in the state are set by central law.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill on 25 March 2026, amending the 2019 Act. The bill was approved by both houses and awaits presidential assent. If assented, it removes the right to legal recognition on the basis of self-identification established by the Supreme Court's 2014 judgment in NALSA v Union of India, confines recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex persons, and otherwise recognises only male and female categories. Trans men, trans women and people who self-identify as gender-fluid or non-binary fall outside the recognition scheme.

Recognition and surgery are made conditional on paperwork. The amendment mandates certification by a medical board and a district authority before gender-affirming surgery, replacing the self-declaration route. It also adds offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring a person to be transgender. The People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that these offences echo the colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The wider baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have read to cover gender identity; there is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership. Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024, when replacement of the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons, and trans people fear a corresponding rise in assaults.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been required by passport authorities to take a medical exam. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities; those bans coexist with clandestine networks still operating.
tangentialFactors:
The 25 March 2026 bill was passed amid protests in Mumbai, and opposition to it is organised rather than isolated: the People's Union for Civil Liberties frames the new offences as a return to the colonial-era regime that targeted transgender people specifically.

Facilities and welfare are largely set at state level, and Haryāna has not been sourced on any of them. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. A visitor should not assume comparable provision in Haryāna on the strength of those examples.

The same divergence seen in police conduct applies to care: Madras High Court and National Medical Commission bans on conversion therapy issued in 2021 and 2022 sit alongside evidence of clandestine networks continuing to operate.
localsOnly:
Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, which reaches residents of Haryāna on the same terms as elsewhere in India.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Residents seeking recognition, surgery or a changed marker will face the certification route set out in the 2026 amendment, once assented: medical-board and district-authority certification, and recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex persons.

Intersex residents remain exposed. Reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations; the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants, an order that binds that state and not Haryāna.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the 2026 amendment is unresolved as of the latest source: it has been passed by both houses of Parliament and awaits presidential assent, so the recognition rules described above may or may not be in force when a visitor travels.

No source in the inventory records Haryāna-specific enforcement of transgender law, police treatment of trans people in the state, document-refusal or airport-stop incidents in the state, or the operation of welfare boards, housing subsidies or pensions there. Whether Haryāna runs a transgender welfare board is not sourced.

Police-conduct assessments conflict and cannot be reconciled from the available material: the United Kingdom's December 2025 note describes abuse as limited and non-systemic, while June 2024 victim interviews document abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

The scale of clandestine conversion-therapy practice is not sourced, including for Haryāna; the inventory establishes that bans exist and that networks continue to operate, without figures.
